When a resident calls me about a skin lesion, I need to see it in my head before the end of the first sentence. So I teach one order, and I ask for it every single time. How many, how big, what shape, what color, what surface, and then where. For example: two small, round, erythematous papules on the left cheek. Or: a three-centimeter, well-defined, scaly plaque on the right elbow. Notice two things. First, all the adjectives come before the noun. Many international residents put them after, because that is natural in their language, and I hear things like a plaque erythematous. Second, when a number and a measure come before the noun, they work as one adjective. So it is a two-centimeter plaque, with a hyphen and no plural. The location comes last, with a preposition. If you describe a lesion this way, I can make a decision on the phone. If you don't, I have to come in at midnight, and nobody is happy.

On my third night on call, a patient came in with a lesion on his scalp, and I wanted my attending to see it. I took a photo, but the hospital system was down, and the photo never arrived. So the description had to do all the work. I was nervous, and I started badly. I said, there is a nodule, skin color, of one centimeter, with an ulcer. My attending was patient. She said: again, in order. So I took a breath and said: a one-centimeter, dome-shaped, skin-colored nodule on the scalp, with a small ulcerated center. There was a short silence, and then she said: perfect, biopsy it in the morning. The biopsy showed a basal cell carcinoma, and it was removed with clear margins. I still think about that night. The medicine was easy. The difficult part was saying it in the right order, and the right order is what made the decision possible.
